To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

phylogenetic congruency between subtropical tree species and their associated soil and foliar pathogenic fungi suggests either diffuse co‐evolution among the tree‐fungi interaction networks or the distribution of fungal pathogens tracked spatially associated host tree species with phylogenetically conservative traits and habitat preferences, which is integral in maintaining biodiversity of forest community.

we found phylogenetic signals for host–fungus interactions, which clustered on the phylogenies of the hosts and the fungi, suggesting that fungal species tracked phylogenetically conscribed traits of their hosts, which may promote host and parasite specificity and maintain the biodiversity of subtropical forests.
the phylogenetic signal in host–fungal networks was detected for both soil‐inhabiting and foliar fungi.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the phylogenetic congruences of host trees and their potential fungal associates.
the phylogenetic patterns of plant–fungus interactions in subtropical forests and the implications of such patterns on the maintenance of plant species diversity.
the phylogenetic congruences between host trees and their associated foliar and soil fungi.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the phylogeny and distribution of fungal species are not random but rather are congruent with the phylogenic and spatial distribution patterns of their host trees, suggesting either coevolution or phylogenetic tracking of host trees.
fungal pathogens of trees are phylogenetically conscribed to their host trees, which may have a significant influence on the coevolution of host and pathogen species.
the phylogenetic signal in the pathogen–host network is a result of the spatially associated hosts that have conserved phylogenetically traits and habitat preferences.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the host–fungus phylogenetic congruency in the subtropical forest community is driven by the spatial distribution of the host species and their phylogenetic conservatism in habitat preferences, which may be a consequence of the coexistence of the host–fungi species.

the phylogenetic congruences among subtropical tree species and their associated fungi are likely to be a consequence of the spatially associated hosts and their phylogenetically conspired traits and habitat preferences rather than coevolution.
the phylogenetic congruency of subtropical trees and associated fungi is due to both coevolutionary and biogeographical processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the phylogenetic relationships among the hosts and their associated pathogens can be used to infer coevolutionary history of the host–pathogen interactions and to predict future pathogen–host associations.
the distribution of fungi within a local community may be constrained by the spatial distribution of hosts.
phylogenetic congruency is not only found between host and pathogen, as has been shown in previous studies, but also between different pathogens and different hosts.
